Inspired by calculator/research workflows in https://github.com/Jera-Value/awesome-investing-tools-and-software-directory, filtered to Legacy Investing Show topics. External brokers, options-flow terminals, and crypto tools were excluded.

tools.title: Cost segregation savings
tools.question: How much extra year-one depreciation tax savings could a study produce?
tools.description: Estimate first-year tax savings from reclassifying rental basis into short-life property, bonus depreciation, and a study fee.
tools.headlineLabel: Year-one tax savings after study cost
tools.formula: Extra dep ≈ bonus on reclassified basis + remaining short-life dep − 27.5-year straight line. Savings = extra dep × tax rate − study cost.
assumptions: Building recovery is 27.5-year straight line with no mid-month convention.
Reclassified property uses a 5-year remainder after bonus.
This does not test passive-activity, at-risk, or taxable-income limits.
howTo: Start with purchase basis and a conservative land percentage.
Enter the share a study would likely move into personal property or land improvements.
Stress the tax rate. If a few points of rate flip the net, get a real quote.
mistakes: Modeling bonus you cannot use because of passive or taxable-income limits.
Ignoring recapture when you sell.
Treating the study cost as optional documentation.

faqs.q: Is this a cost segregation study?
faqs.a: No. It is a planning screen so you can decide whether to price a study. The study creates the allocations your CPA files.

faqs.q: What bonus rate should I use in 2026?
faqs.a: Qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025 can use 100% bonus. Confirm placed-in-service dates with your advisor.

faqs.q: Do I need to be a real estate professional?
faqs.a: Not always. Short-term rental material participation can matter more for W-2 owners. This calculator does not test those hours.

tools.title: 1031 exchange deferred gain
tools.question: How much gain is deferred if you replace a rental and how much boot is taxed now?
tools.description: Estimate realized gain, boot, and deferred gain on a like-kind rental exchange using sale price, basis, and replacement price.
tools.formula: Realized gain = sale price − selling costs − adjusted basis. Recognized gain = min(realized gain, boot). Deferred = realized − recognized.
assumptions: Both properties are like-kind investment real estate.
Boot is the greater of cash kept and equity not rolled into the replacement.
Identification and closing deadlines are not modeled.
howTo: Use the actual sale price and a realistic cost of sale.
Enter adjusted basis after depreciation, not original purchase price.
If you keep cash or buy down, put it in boot.
mistakes: Using original purchase price as basis.
Forgetting selling costs, which reduce realized gain.
Treating a vacation home as automatically like-kind.

faqs.a: Value you take out of the exchange: cash, debt relief you do not replace, or a cheaper replacement. Boot can make part of the gain taxable now.
No. It usually reduces basis in the replacement property and shows up later on sale unless you exchange again.
It depends on use, holding, and whether it is investment property. Confirm with a QI and a CPA before you list.

tools.title: Bonus depreciation estimate
tools.question: What year-one deduction does a bonus percentage create on qualifying basis?
tools.description: Turn qualifying short-life rental or business basis into an estimated bonus depreciation deduction and tax savings.
tools.formula: Bonus = qualifying basis × bonus%. Tax savings = bonus × tax rate.
assumptions: The basis is already eligible (typically 5, 7, or 15-year property).
No taxable-income or passive-loss limitation is applied.
2026 planning default is 100% for qualifying post-January 19, 2025 property.
howTo: Use the personal-property or improvement basis, not the whole building.
Set bonus to the rate that applies to the placed-in-service year.
If you cannot use the loss this year, lower the tax-rate assumption.
mistakes: Applying bonus to land or 27.5-year residential rental structure.
Ignoring that unused losses may be suspended.
Forgetting recapture on sale or conversion.

faqs.q: Is furniture for an Airbnb bonus property?
faqs.a: Often yes if it is personal property used in the business and placed in service. Keep invoices.

faqs.q: Does bonus replace a cost-seg study?
faqs.a: No. Bonus needs a qualifying asset class. The study is how you support moving building costs into those classes.

faqs.q: What if my bonus year is not 100%?
faqs.a: Enter the percentage that applies to your placed-in-service date.

tools.title: Depreciation recapture
tools.question: How much of a rental sale is recapture versus long-term capital gain?
tools.description: Split a rental sale into depreciation recapture and leftover long-term gain using basis, accumulated depreciation, and your rates.
tools.headlineLabel: Estimated federal tax on the sale
tools.formula: Gain = amount realized − (original basis − accumulated depreciation). Recapture = min(gain, accumulated depreciation).
assumptions: Residential rental recapture is modeled at the rate you enter, default 25% unrecaptured 1250.
State tax, NIIT, and 1245 personal-property recapture at ordinary rates are not auto-split.
Installment sales and 1031 exchanges are excluded.
howTo: Pull accumulated depreciation from prior returns or depreciation schedules.
Use 25% unless your CPA tells you a different mix of 1245 and 1250.
Compare this result to a 1031 if you are not done owning rentals.
mistakes: Reporting the whole gain at 15%.
Forgetting selling costs.
Ignoring NIIT on high MAGI years.

faqs.a: Unrecaptured 1250 on real property is generally capped at 25%. Personal property (1245) can be ordinary. This tool uses the rate you enter for the recapture slice.
A valid exchange can defer it. Recapture can still matter later.
Not included. Add 3.8% mentally if MAGI is over the NIIT threshold.

tools.title: Quarterly estimated tax
tools.question: What should each remaining estimated payment be, and what does safe harbor require?
tools.description: Split remaining federal tax across the payments you still have to make, and compare that plan to last year's safe-harbor target.
tools.formula: Remaining tax = annual estimate − already paid. Payment = remaining tax ÷ remaining payments. Safe harbor = last year × 100% or 110%.
assumptions: This is a cash plan, not Form 2210 annualization.
High-income safe harbor is modeled as 110% of last year's tax when the toggle is 1.
Penalties, state estimates, and household employment tax are excluded.
howTo: Update the annual estimate whenever profit or withholding changes.
Count only payments still ahead of you, including the next due date.
If income is lumpy, compare this with a CPA annualized method.
mistakes: Ignoring withholding, which is treated as paid evenly.
Using four payments when Q1 already passed.
Assuming safe harbor equals what you will actually owe.

faqs.q: Should I use safe harbor or the current-year number?
faqs.a: Safe harbor is the simpler penalty floor. Pay the higher of a realistic current-year remainder and the safe-harbor remainder if you want margin.
Higher AGI filers often must use 110% of last year's tax. Set the toggle to 1 if that is you.
Only if you put it in the annual estimate. Pair with the self-employment tax reserve tool.

related.question: When lumpy income changes the method.

tools.title: QBI deduction estimate
tools.question: What 20% qualified business income deduction survives a simple wage limitation?
tools.description: Estimate Section 199A QBI as the lesser of 20% of QBI, 20% of taxable income, and optionally 50% of W-2 wages.
tools.formula: QBI deduction ≈ min(20% × QBI, 20% × taxable income, and if toggled 50% × W-2 wages).
assumptions: Specified-service trade or business phaseouts are not modeled.
The UBIA 2.5% property test is not modeled.
Turn on the wage limit if you are over the taxable-income threshold.
howTo: Use profit after ordinary business deductions, not gross receipts.
If you are well under the threshold, leave the wage limit off.
If you are over it, turn the limit on and see whether wages or QBI binds.
mistakes: Treating W-2 wages paid to yourself in an S corp as increasing QBI. They reduce QBI.
Ignoring SSTB phaseouts for consultants and similar fields.
Using AGI instead of taxable income.

faqs.q: Does an S corp help QBI?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Reasonable salary creates wages that can support the limitation, but salary itself is not QBI. Model both.
They can be if they rise to a trade or business. That is facts-and-circumstances. Do not assume it.
No. Taxable income and wage/property tests can cut it. This is the simple screen.

tools.title: S corp vs sole prop tax
tools.question: How much self-employment tax might an S corp salary split save versus Schedule C?
tools.description: Compare sole-proprietor SE tax with employer-plus-employee FICA on a reasonable S corp salary using 2026 Social Security wage-base math.
tools.headlineLabel: Payroll / SE tax saved with an S corp
tools.formula: Sole-prop SE ≈ 15.3% of 92.35% of profit (SS capped). S corp FICA ≈ 15.3% of salary (SS capped). Savings = SE − FICA.
assumptions: 2026 Social Security wage base is $184,500.
Additional Medicare uses the $200,000 single threshold.
Income tax, QBI, reasonable-salary risk, and payroll service costs are excluded.
howTo: Use profit after ordinary expenses, before owner draws.
Set salary to something you can defend with role, hours, and comps.
If savings are smaller than payroll friction, stay on Schedule C.
mistakes: Setting salary near zero.
Forgetting employer FICA is a real check you write.
Ignoring QBI wage effects.

faqs.q: Is this the full S corp analysis?
faqs.a: No. It isolates payroll tax. Income tax, QBI, state unemployment, and administration can erase a thin savings number.
What you would pay someone else to do the owner work. Document it.

faqs.q: Does this include the 20% QBI deduction?
faqs.a: No. Pair it with the QBI estimate.

related.question: When the election is worth the friction.

tools.title: FIRE number
tools.question: What portfolio would cover your spending at the withdrawal rate you choose?
tools.description: Translate annual spending into a FIRE / Coast-style portfolio target using a sustainable withdrawal rate, then show the gap versus what you have.
tools.formula: Target = annual spending ÷ (withdrawal rate ÷ 100). 4% implies 25× spending.
assumptions: Spending is real, after-tax lifestyle cost, not gross income.
The withdrawal rate is a planning lever, not a guarantee.
Pensions, Social Security, and rental cash flow are not subtracted unless you lower spending.
howTo: Use a year of actual spending, not a hopeful budget.
If rentals will keep running, reduce spending by the cash you trust.
Compare 3.5%, 4%, and 5% before you treat the target as a date.
mistakes: Using gross income instead of spending.
Ignoring sequence-of-returns risk in the first decade.
Counting the house you live in as the whole portfolio.

faqs.a: Because 4% of 25× spending is one year of spending. Lower rates need a larger multiple.
Include the equity only if you would sell or refinance them. Otherwise subtract trusted cash flow from spending.
It is a research starting point, not a promise. Fees, taxes, and a bad first decade all matter.

tools.title: 4% rule withdrawal
tools.question: What first-year withdrawal does your portfolio support at the rate you choose?
tools.description: Apply a withdrawal rate to invested assets to estimate a first-year retirement paycheck and the implied portfolio multiple.
tools.formula: Withdrawal = portfolio × rate. Multiple = 100 ÷ rate.
assumptions: This is year-one spending, not an inflation-adjusted path.
Taxes and fees are not subtracted.
Sequence risk is not simulated.
howTo: Use investable assets, not home equity you will not sell.
Try 3.5% if you retire early with a long horizon.
If rentals cover part of spending, you can take less from the portfolio.
mistakes: Withdrawing 4% of a peak balance after a crash.
Forgetting taxes on pretax accounts.
Treating the rule as a legal guarantee.

faqs.q: Is the 4% rule the same as FIRE?
faqs.a: FIRE uses it as a target. This tool is the spending side of that coin.

faqs.q: Do I raise it with inflation?
faqs.a: Many research versions inflate the first-year amount. This page shows year one only.
Add it outside the portfolio. It can let you draw less.

tools.title: Rule of 72
tools.question: How long until this return doubles the money, and what is the exact compound time?
tools.description: Estimate doubling time with the Rule of 72 and show the exact compound-interest years next to it.
tools.formula: Rule of 72 years = 72 ÷ annual percent return. Exact years = ln(2) ÷ ln(1 + r).
assumptions: Return is constant and compounds annually.
Taxes, fees, and contributions are ignored.
The Rule of 72 is an approximation; the exact line is also shown.
howTo: Use a net-of-fee expected return, not a best year.
Compare 6%, 8%, and 10% so you do not treat one rate as fate.
If you add money monthly, use compound savings growth instead.
mistakes: Using a 20% year as if it repeats.
Ignoring fees, which are a direct cut to the rate.
Applying it to a leveraged deal with principal risk.

faqs.a: It is a mental-math approximation that stays close for common rates around 6% to 10%.
Use a real return if you want doubling of purchasing power.

faqs.q: How do investment fees change doubling?
faqs.a: A 1% fee on an 8% return is a 7% return. Plug the net number.

tools.title: Dividend reinvestment
tools.question: What could reinvested dividends and monthly adds grow to at a constant yield?
tools.description: Project a dividend or yield portfolio with DRIP and optional monthly contributions at a constant annual yield.
tools.formula: FV = principal × (1+r)^n + annual adds × ((1+r)^n − 1) / r, with r as yield.
assumptions: Yield is constant and fully reinvested.
Price changes, dividend cuts, and taxes are ignored.
Monthly additions are treated as an annual end-of-year contribution equal to 12 months.
howTo: Use a net yield after foreign tax and fund expense if you want a conservative line.
If you spend the dividends, set monthly add to 0 and treat yield as income instead.
Compare with compound savings growth if total return matters more than yield.
mistakes: Assuming a 8% stock yield with no cut risk.
Ignoring that reinvested dividends are often taxable in a brokerage account.
Counting yield and price growth twice.

faqs.a: It compounds the yield you enter. If you want price growth too, raise the rate or use the compound savings tool.
In a Roth, the projection is closer to spendable. In taxable, haircut the yield.

faqs.q: What yield should a diversified investor use?
faqs.a: Broad equity indexes are often in the 1% to 2% range. Higher yields usually mean more concentration or more risk.

tools.title: Roth vs Traditional
tools.question: Which account wins after tax if rates today and in retirement are different?
tools.description: Compare Roth and Traditional future after-tax values for the same contribution and for the same paycheck cost.
tools.headlineLabel: Roth advantage on the same paycheck
tools.formula: Traditional after-tax FV = FV × (1 − retirement rate). Same-paycheck Roth invests contribution × (1 − current rate).
assumptions: One lump contribution compounds annually. No employer match.
Retirement withdrawals are taxed at a single marginal rate.
NIIT, IRMAA, and pro-rata Roth conversion rules are excluded.
howTo: Use current marginal rate, not effective rate.
If you expect lower brackets in retirement, Traditional often wins on the same dollar.
Read the same-paycheck row if Roth contributions come from after-tax cash.
mistakes: Comparing a $23k Roth with a $23k Traditional as equal paycheck cost.
Ignoring a match, which is usually pretax.
Using average tax rate in retirement for a large conversion year.

faqs.a: When you expect a higher rate later, or you want tax-free flexibility and are paying tax from cash you would not have invested anyway.
This is the growth comparison, not the pro-rata test.

faqs.q: Should high-income W-2s always pick Traditional?
faqs.a: Often for the deduction, then convert in lower-income years. It is a sequence, not a forever choice.

tools.title: HELOC payment
tools.question: What is the interest-only cost of a drawn HELOC versus a fully amortizing payment?
tools.description: Compare interest-only and amortizing payments on a drawn home-equity line, plus total interest if you amortize the draw.
tools.formula: Interest-only = draw × rate ÷ 12. Amortizing = standard mortgage payment on the draw.
assumptions: Rate is fixed for the comparison. Real HELOCs often adjust.
Draw period vs repayment period is not staged.
Tax deductibility is not assumed.
howTo: Use the amount you would actually draw, not the full limit.
Stress a higher rate. HELOC risk is the reset.
If this is a down-payment bridge, pair it with a written payoff date.
mistakes: Comparing interest-only to a mortgage without noticing principal is not being paid.
Ignoring closing costs on a cash-out refinance alternative.
Using teaser rate as the life rate.

faqs.a: Only in some cases, usually when the funds buy or improve the secured home. Ask a CPA; this page is cash flow.
Refi resets the first mortgage. A HELOC stacks a second lien. Payment shape is not the only risk.

faqs.q: What about a Solo 401(k) loan instead?
faqs.a: Different collateral and opportunity cost. See the related comparison page.

tools.title: PMI removal
tools.question: How many months until the loan reaches 80% LTV so PMI can drop?
tools.description: Amortize a mortgage with optional extra principal to estimate when LTV hits 80% and how much PMI you still pay before then.
tools.formula: Each month: balance -= scheduled principal + extra. Stop when balance ÷ value ≤ 80%.
assumptions: Value is held constant. Appreciation is not modeled.
80% LTV is the borrower-requested removal target, not automatic 78% termination.
Lender seasoning, appraisal, and automatic termination rules vary.
howTo: Use today's balance and a conservative value, not list price.
If extra principal is zero, you are waiting on scheduled amortization only.
Ask the servicer whether they need an appraisal at 80%.
mistakes: Using original purchase price after a price drop.
Forgetting PMI does not automatically vanish at 80% on all loans.
Counting a cash-out refinance as removal without modeling the new loan.

faqs.a: Borrowers can often request cancellation at 80% LTV. Automatic termination is commonly 78% of original value. Confirm with the servicer.

faqs.q: Does extra payment always win vs investing?
faqs.a: Only if the after-tax PMI plus mortgage rate beats expected invested return. Pair with the mortgage vs index tool.

faqs.q: What if value rose a lot?
faqs.a: Raise the value input. That can hit 80% without extra payments.

tools.title: Extra payment priority
tools.question: Should extra cash hit the mortgage or higher-rate consumer debt first?
tools.description: Compare lifetime interest saved if the same extra monthly payment goes to the mortgage versus a consumer loan or card.
tools.formula: Amortize each balance with and without the extra payment. Interest saved = baseline interest − accelerated interest.
assumptions: Each path applies the entire extra payment to one balance.
Rates stay fixed.
Tax deductibility of mortgage interest is ignored, which favors the consumer-debt path if you itemize.
howTo: If the card rate is double-digit, it almost always wins.
If consumer debt is already small, check months saved, not just dollars.
After the expensive balance is gone, rerun with investing vs extra mortgage.
mistakes: Paying 6% mortgage extra while carrying 21% cards.
Counting expected market returns as guaranteed.
Ignoring the emergency fund before extra principal.

faqs.q: What if the consumer loan is 0% promo?
faqs.a: Set the consumer rate to 0 and the mortgage will win on interest. Watch the promo end date.
After high-rate debt is gone, compare extra mortgage to index investing.

faqs.q: Does this include the snowball method?
faqs.a: This is avalanche math: rate first. Use snowball vs avalanche for multiple cards.

tools.title: Credit utilization
tools.question: What percent of revolving limits is used, and how much paydown reaches 30% or 10%?
tools.description: Calculate revolving utilization and the paydown needed to reach common 30% and 10% scoring guardrails.
tools.formula: Utilization = balances ÷ limits. Paydown to 30% = max(0, balances − 0.3 × limits).
assumptions: Installment loans are excluded. This is revolving utilization.
Scoring models differ; 30% and 10% are planning guardrails, not official cutoffs.
Authorized-user and business-card treatment varies.
howTo: Use statement balances the bureaus are likely to see, not today's app balance if it has not reported.
If you are applying for a mortgage, 10% is a cleaner target than 30%.
Paying before the statement date often helps more than paying after.
mistakes: Closing old cards and shrinking limits.
Maxing a store card while overall utilization looks fine.
Carrying a balance to 'build credit' at 20%+ APR.

faqs.a: Very low is good. Some people keep a small reported balance so the file shows activity. Do not pay interest for that.
Not in this revolving ratio. They hit DTI instead.

faqs.q: Will this raise my score by X points?
faqs.a: No model here can promise points. It shows the ratio lenders still quote.

examples.name: High util
examples.description: One maxed card in the mix.

tools.title: STR break-even occupancy
tools.question: What occupancy keeps a short-term rental from losing money at this nightly rate?
tools.description: Convert monthly STR costs and ADR into the occupancy rate that covers the operation after platform fees.
tools.formula: Nights needed = monthly costs ÷ (ADR × (1 − fee%)). Occupancy = nights needed ÷ (365/12).

inputs.label: Fixed monthly costs (rent or PITI + ops)

assumptions: Guest-paid cleaning is assumed to offset cleaners and is not in ADR.
Costs include the lease or mortgage plus utilities, software, and supplies you actually pay.
No seasonality curve: one ADR all year.
howTo: Put every cost that does not vanish on a vacant night into monthly costs.
Use trailing ADR, not a peak-weekend screenshot.
If break-even occupancy is above realistic market occupancy, the deal is too tight.
mistakes: Leaving rent out of costs on an arbitrage deal.
Using 100% occupancy as the plan.
Adding cleaning fees into ADR.

faqs.q: Is this the same as the Airbnb ROI calculator?
faqs.a: That tool is a full cash-on-cash model. This one answers the single occupancy question operators actually argue about.
It is market-specific. If you cannot defend it with comps, do not underwrite it.
If furniture and appliances will be replaced, add a monthly reserve to costs.

tools.title: STR ADR needed
tools.question: What nightly rate covers costs and your target profit at this occupancy?
tools.description: Solve for the average daily rate an STR needs after platform fees, given occupancy, monthly costs, and a profit target.
tools.formula: ADR = ((monthly costs + target profit) ÷ occupied nights) ÷ (1 − fee%).
assumptions: Occupied nights = occupancy × 365/12.
Profit is cash after the costs you entered, not after tax.
Dynamic pricing is collapsed into one ADR.
howTo: Set target profit to 0 to see pure break-even ADR.
If comps cannot print this ADR, cut costs or skip the lease.
Run a winter occupancy, not just summer.
mistakes: Using 80% occupancy in a market that prints 55%.
Forgetting owner stays, which are occupancy without ADR.
Treating a listing's 'similar listings' map as a comp set.

faqs.a: This solves ADR. Revenue per available night is ADR × occupancy.
Keep guest-paid cleaning out of ADR if it only offsets the cleaner.

faqs.q: Can I hit this with weekly discounts?
faqs.a: Then your true ADR is lower. Enter the blended number.

tools.title: STR cleaning & turnover
tools.question: What do turnovers really cost each month once cleaner, supplies, and laundry are included?
tools.description: Multiply monthly turnovers by cleaner, supplies, and laundry to see the operating cost most STR spreadsheets understate.
tools.formula: Monthly cost = turnovers × (cleaner + supplies + laundry).
assumptions: Guest-paid cleaning fees may offset the cleaner line. If they do, set cleaner to your net.
Owner-hours are not priced unless you put a dollar amount in cleaner.
Damage and deep cleans are extra.
howTo: Count actual turnovers from the last 90 days, not a hope.
If you self-clean, still enter a wage you would pay someone else.
High turnover with thin ADR is how arbitrage dies.
mistakes: Assuming the cleaning fee is profit.
Ignoring laundry on back-to-back nights.
Underwriting 15 turnovers at a 2-hour self-clean.

faqs.q: Should the guest cleaning fee be income?
faqs.a: Usually it is an offset to this cost, not extra profit.
Booked nights ÷ average stay length. A 2-night average stay at 60% occupancy is a lot of cleans.
Yes. Fewer turnovers is the whole point of the midterm comparison.

tools.title: Midterm vs STR
tools.question: Does nightly STR net more than a furnished midterm lease after fees and ops?
tools.description: Compare monthly net from a short-term rental versus a midterm furnished rental using occupancy, fees, vacancy, and operating costs.
tools.headlineLabel: Monthly edge for STR vs midterm
tools.formula: STR net = ADR × occupancy × days × (1 − fees) − STR ops. Midterm net = rent × (1 − vacancy) − midterm ops.
assumptions: Rent or PITI is excluded from both ops so the comparison is operating style, not financing.
Add the same housing cost to both sides mentally, or include it in both ops if you prefer.
Regulation risk is not priced.
howTo: Use winter STR occupancy, not July.
Put cleaning and software in STR ops.
If STR wins by $200, that is not a mandate. It is a fragile edge.
mistakes: Comparing STR gross to midterm net.
Leaving utilities out of STR ops.
Ignoring 30-day minimum laws.

faqs.a: It is the same property either way. The difference is revenue quality and ops.

faqs.q: What occupancy voids an STR win?
faqs.a: Drop occupancy in this form until the edge flips. That is your risk number.
Usually fewer turns, more credit risk, different insurance. This page is only the cash comparison.

tools.title: Cap rate
tools.question: What capitalization rate does this rental's NOI produce at the price you would pay?
tools.description: Divide annual net operating income by purchase price to get cap rate and the years of NOI needed to recover price.
tools.formula: Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price.
assumptions: NOI is rent minus operating expenses and vacancy, before debt service.
Cap rate is not cash-on-cash and ignores financing.
Appreciation is excluded.
howTo: Build NOI from trailing rent and real expenses, not the listing's pro forma.
If the seller quotes a cap, rebuild NOI yourself.
Compare cap to local debt cost. A 5% cap with 7% money is a leverage warning.
mistakes: Using net cash flow after the mortgage as NOI.
Leaving out taxes, insurance, and management.
Comparing cap rates across markets with different risk.

faqs.q: Is a higher cap always better?
faqs.a: It usually means more risk, more deferred maintenance, or a cheaper market. Read the NOI quality.

faqs.q: Does cap rate include the loan?
faqs.a: No. That is cash-on-cash and DSCR.
Use a conservative net, not a peak-season annualization.

tools.title: Cash-on-cash return
tools.question: What cash-on-cash return remains after vacancy, operating costs, and debt service?
tools.description: Turn monthly rent, vacancy, ops, and debt service into annual cash flow divided by cash invested.
tools.formula: Annual CF = (rent × (1 − vacancy%) − ops − debt) × 12. CoC = annual CF ÷ cash invested.
assumptions: Operating costs exclude the mortgage, which has its own field.
Capex reserves belong in ops if you want an honest CoC.
Tax effects are excluded.
howTo: Cash invested is down payment plus closing plus initial capex.
If CoC looks spectacular, the denominator is probably too small or ops are incomplete.
Compare with cap rate to see how much of the return is leverage.
mistakes: Using purchase price instead of cash in.
Zero vacancy forever.
Leaving management out because you will self-manage.

faqs.q: Why is CoC higher than cap rate?
faqs.a: Leverage. It can also go negative faster when rates rise.
Only if the cash flow survives a vacancy and a repair year. Percentage without a stress test is a slogan.
Yes if cash in is deposits and furnishings. The Airbnb ROI tool is the fuller version.

tools.title: DSCR
tools.question: Does net operating income cover the annual mortgage by the ratio a DSCR lender wants?
tools.description: Estimate debt-service coverage ratio from annual NOI and an amortizing loan's principal-and-interest payment.
tools.formula: DSCR = annual NOI ÷ (monthly P&I × 12).
assumptions: Payment is P&I only. Taxes and insurance in NOI should already be expensed.
Interest-only DSCR loans would show a higher ratio; this uses full amortization.
Lender haircuts to income are not applied.
howTo: Many DSCR programs want 1.0 to 1.25. If you are at 0.95, the file is fragile.
Rebuild NOI from leases, not the broker OM.
Raise rate 100 bps and see if the ratio still clears.
mistakes: Using gross rent instead of NOI.
Comparing to a 1.25 requirement with an interest-only quote you will not keep.
Ignoring impounds that do not sit in NOI.

faqs.a: It varies. 1.0 is a common floor; 1.25 is a healthier file. Ask the actual program.

faqs.q: Does this include taxes and insurance?
faqs.a: They should already be in NOI as expenses. Do not subtract them again from debt service unless your lender uses PITIA in the denominator.
Lenders often haircut it. Use a lower NOI.

tools.title: BRRRR analysis
tools.question: How much cash stays in a buy-rehab-rent-refinance deal, and what cash flow is left?
tools.description: Estimate cash left in after an ARV refinance, then monthly cash flow and cash-on-cash on the remaining cash.
tools.formula: Cash left in = purchase + rehab − ARV × refi LTV. Cash flow uses the new amortizing payment.
assumptions: Refinance closes at the ARV and LTV you enter. Appraisal risk is not simulated.
Purchase closing costs live inside rehab/holding if you put them there.
Seasoning rules and cash-out limits vary by lender.
howTo: If cash left in is negative, the deal cash-out refinances. Confirm the lender allows it.
ARV is the number that makes or breaks BRRRR. Be boring.
Rerun at 70% LTV if 75% feels like a brochure.
mistakes: Using retail ARV on a house that will still look like a rehab.
Forgetting holding costs during rehab.
Underwriting rent from Zillow without comps.

faqs.q: What if cash left in is negative?
faqs.a: You pulled money out. CoC is not a useful percentage then; look at cash flow and risk.
Sometimes. Many investors underwrite 70% so the refinance still closes.

faqs.q: Does this include the original hard-money loan?
faqs.a: No. It assumes you get to the long-term refinance. Bridge costs belong in rehab/holding.

tools.title: House hack cash flow
tools.question: What is your net housing cost after rent from other units or rooms?
tools.description: Subtract effective rent from housemates or extra units from PITI and owner-occupied operating costs to see what housing actually costs.
tools.formula: Net housing = PITI + owner ops − rent × (1 − vacancy%).
assumptions: You still live in the property. This is housing cost, not a pure investment CoC.
Vacancy applies only to the rented portion.
Tax benefits of owner-occupied vs rental allocation are excluded.
howTo: Use PITI from the mortgage tool, not a round number from memory.
If you rent rooms, vacancy is roommate turnover.
A negative net housing cost means the property pays you to live there — until a void month.
mistakes: Ignoring that you still need a bedroom when the tenant leaves.
Underwriting 100% occupancy on three rooms in a house you also occupy.
Forgetting utilities you agreed to cover.

faqs.q: Is house hacking the same as a duplex rental?
faqs.a: You occupy part of it. Financing and tax treatment differ from a pure rental.

faqs.q: Can this be an STR on the other unit?
faqs.a: Yes, but then use STR occupancy and ops, not a simple vacancy percent.
Some lenders count a fraction of rental income. Do not assume 100% of this rent lands on the application.
